title: Farmers March in Sambhajinagar as Congress Calls Rs 5,000 Drought Aid Too Little
excerpt: Thousands joined the Congress Jan Aakrosh drought march led by Harshwardhan Sapkal, who demands Rs 50,000 per hectare and a loan waiver; the government calls its Rs 5,000 a first-ever advance paid ahead of full assessment.
body:
• Thousands of farmers joined the Congress party's Jan Aakrosh drought march in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, led by state Congress chief Harshwardhan Sapkal.
  • Sapkal has demanded Rs 50,000 per hectare paid directly to farmers, plus a blanket loan waiver — far above the government's Rs 5,000 advance.
  • The state has declared drought in 305 of 358 talukas and says the Rs 5,000 is an advance, paid before Diwali because central assessment cannot finish in time.
  • The government says about 1 to 1.25 crore farmers will receive the advance, an outlay of roughly Rs 6,000 crore, with loan-waiver credits also under way.

Maharashtra's drought has moved from the cabinet room to the street. Thousands of farmers and residents joined a Jan Aakrosh (public anger) drought march organised by the Maharashtra Congress in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, as the opposition attacked the state government's Rs 5,000 pre-Diwali payment to drought-hit farmers as inadequate against crop losses across 305 declared drought-hit talukas.

State Congress president Harshwardhan Sapkal led the march alongside former minister Balasaheb Thorat and MP Kalyan Kale, with MLAs, MPs and district party leaders also taking part, according to reports of the demonstration. The march follows Sapkal's public question to the government — how farmers are expected to celebrate Diwali with Rs 5,000 after a failed season.

What the opposition is demanding

The Congress demand is an order of magnitude larger than the government's offer. Sapkal has called for the drought to be met with Rs 50,000 per hectare credited directly into farmers' bank accounts and a blanket loan waiver, warning in earlier statements reported by IANS that ministers would face public anger if relief did not arrive promptly. He has argued that standing crops withered after more than a month without rain in several districts, and accused the BJP-led Mahayuti government of holding cabinet discussions without taking concrete decisions while guardian ministers failed to visit affected farmers.

"How can farmers celebrate Diwali with Rs 5,000?"

— Harshwardhan Sapkal, Maharashtra Congress President

The Sambhajinagar march is the street-level expression of that argument: a demand that relief be scaled to the loss — per hectare of damaged crop — rather than paid as a flat festival advance.

The government's position

Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has presented the Rs 5,000 differently: not as final compensation, but as a first-ever advance, paid ahead of the full assessment because the standard process cannot legally conclude before Diwali. The state initially declared 265 talukas drought-hit and added 40 more after reviewing complaints, taking the total to 305 of 358 talukas — more than 85 percent of the state — with all 12 standard drought concessions extended to them, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

Fadnavis said drought assistance is normally paid in December and that the government moved the declaration forward this year, adding that loan-waiver amounts are also being credited. Government sources cited by ANI put the advance's reach at roughly 1 to 1.25 crore farmers and its cost at about Rs 6,000 crore, with the final central assistance to follow when it arrives. The government has also said the model code of conduct does not block drought-relief meetings or measures.

What happens next

The immediate test is mechanical: whether the Rs 5,000 advance reaches bank accounts before Diwali, as promised. The political test runs longer. The opposition's per-hectare demand and the loan-waiver call now have a visible protest behind them, while the government is betting that speed — money before the festival, months ahead of the usual December timeline — answers the charge of indifference. For farming families in the 305 talukas, the gap between the two numbers, Rs 5,000 now against Rs 50,000 per hectare demanded, is the argument that will decide how this Diwali is remembered. Readers can follow our earlier coverage of the declaration in Maharashtra Declares Drought in 305 Talukas.
